What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. #9932. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.
