#9931. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, But Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9930. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI)

Nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows.

Niko Matsakis is one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language and co-lead of the Rust language design team. He is a Senior Principal Engineer at Amazon and a Project Director on the Rust Foundation Board. He is the creator of Symposium, an open-source platform for agent mods built on the Agent Client Protocol.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Niko Matsakis: My name is Nicholas Matsakis. I am one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language. I've been working on it since 2011. I also am a senior principal engineer at Amazon. I started there about five years ago, in part because Amazon has been adopting tons of Rust, and I wanted to see it firsthand, see how it was going. I'm going to just show my whole cards with you and just tell you all the things I'm going to tell you. Step one, I'm going to try to convince you that Rust and AI is a really great combination, perhaps better than some of the alternatives out there. I have a project I'm curious to get feedback on that I think makes it even better, which I call Symposium, and covers up some of the gaps I see. Next, that actually, if you look at how Symposium works, what you'll find is it reveals something about the way we're currently building all our development tools here, which is that individual vendors, like Anthropic or OpenAI or whatever, everyone's trying to build a complete tool that solves all the problems, and I want to see us do more of an extensibility story where people can plug in and add things and you have a whole bunch of extensions. I think we're only scraping the surface of what is possible, but it's very difficult to do with the way the tools are set up now. Then I'll talk to you about Agent Client Protocol, which is an interesting way to get past that and get to a more extensible model.

How many have heard of Rust? Rust is all about having a language that can go as low-level as you want, as efficient, give you as much control over the hardware. Low-level enough to be used in a kernel, but be productive. High-level enough that you can write application-level software in it, and it's not too bad. It may not be the minimum line count or what have you, but it's not too bad. Low-level enough for a kernel, I mean that quite literally. We are the only language apart from C, not even C++, that's allowed in the Linux kernel, just C and Rust. Also, we're being used in the Microsoft's kernel and elsewhere. That's been pretty cool. In terms of high-level enough for an application, just to give you some idea, this is a library called ratatui, which is a text user interface library, and they have all kinds of neat little demos.

You're seeing more and more of this user-facing software where performance may not be the number one criteria, but it works really well in Rust, and then it does scale up to crazy things like this oscilloscope or whatever that is. I've been giving a lot of talks on Rust for the last 15 years. I was at QCon in Brazil, in Sao Paulo in 2019 giving a talk like this. What I would say is it's sometimes a bit of a tough sell, because Rust's whole premise is like this eat your spinach thing. You know where your parents were like, eat it, it's good for you. We're telling you, Rust is going to make your code faster, it's going to make it more efficient, but it is going to take you a month and a half or three months or however long it's going to be to learn how it works and incorporate those new style of development into your workflow.

People are like, I would like it to go fast, but I want to ship tomorrow, so actually I'm going to stick with TypeScript. I can hire all the people I need. That makes a lot of sense. What I try to tell them is, yes, it is spinach, but it's like Popeyes spinach. You're going to eat it, and then you're going to be stronger, you're going to go faster. It's going to be great. Usually it doesn't win over, but that's changed a lot. What's happened is, if the agent's doing the coding, the agent already learned Rust in its training, its reinforcement learning stages and whatnot. It already passed that stage, so you just get to skip to the Popeyes stage, to the part where you've got this type system that's giving the agent guardrails and helping it stay on track and get programs that are more likely to be correct. You don't have to take it from me. You can take it from Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, who said Rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles, it's approximately correct.

In terms of this range of applications, another thing pulling people in is, like I said, Rust is low-level enough for a kernel, but usable enough for an application. It covers a wide space. You have things like codex-rs, which used to be in TypeScript, being ported over. That's something that's pulling people in. Then, of course, there's the old standby, which is efficiency. If you're building network services or whatnot, where you're paying per load, or maybe you're building a mobile app or something that's going to take your user's battery, then it becomes a really big consideration. You can save quite a bit of money. That's, of course, what's driving Rust at Amazon. We run things at really large scale. It's been fascinating, though, to watch the shift. When I first got there, it's the same as what I told you, people are thinking, Rust is maybe going to take me some time to learn.

I'm only going to use it in the critical data paths. S3, EC2, Lambda, those are the first adopters where the real heavy workloads are driving. Then people get used to it, and they started to use it in more and more places. There's an interesting blog post talking about DSQL, which is this serverless SQL database, and their story where they went through that whole trial. They started with just one narrow part, wound up using Rust in the data plane and the control plane and in their Postgres bindings and the whole thing. What's happening lately, it's really different, except I didn't actually get cleared to talk about all the cool things. Let me tell you about something else, and then we'll come back, where Microsoft is saying we're maybe going to try to do AI-driven rewrites of a million lines of code by one engineer. This is just a research project.

Of course, then Bun is running off, putting it into production where they're taking however many lines of code. I think it was a million, from Zig to Rust. I can neither confirm nor deny that similar experiments are taking place at Amazon and in many FAANG companies that I've been a part of, with, to me, quite surprising rates of success. Basically, it's now possible to move large codebases in a matter of weeks or months, which used to take decades or infinity because it usually failed. What I'm seeing more and more is if this was Rust before, this is Rust now going even faster. That's pretty cool.

There's one other factor, though. I mentioned Rust is like an eat your spinach thing. There's two ways to get people to eat their vegetables. One is that they feel motivated. The other is that the doctor tells them you have six months to live unless you change your dietary habits. That will also be motivating. We're seeing some of that happening now. Maybe when this roadrunner is looking behind him, what he's really looking at is Mythos coming around and saying, it turns out if you're using a memory unsafe language like C or C++, or even languages that make heavy use of really dynamic features like reflection, there's tons of vulnerabilities all scattered throughout your code, and I can help you find them, and I can help your attackers find them, too. That's also pushing a lot of people, I think, towards Rust and just towards generally more statically verifiable languages.

I think this is going to be an accelerating trend. I think we're going to see more and more a need to really get to a high level of validation on your software, because the minute it ships, somebody else can be running an AI against it, especially if it's open source, but even if it's not, if it's reverse-engineerable, and finding vulnerabilities. You really got to have them buttoned down.

This has been a story for a while. Android, this is from a great blog post by the Android team. They've been slowly and steadily, at least in the old days, porting their code from C++ over into Rust. There's a really interesting chart, actually, I think a mixture of Rust and Kotlin. There's a really interesting chart here, the blue line is the amount of new memory unsafe code. The red line is the number of new memory safety related vulnerabilities. You can see there's like a linear relationship. I don't know how long all of you have been in the field, but the entire time that I've been working in this area, 20-plus years, people have cited this statistic that 70% of vulnerabilities are related to memory safety. Nothing has changed it. Nothing. Whether you bring in Coverity or all these static checkers and all this other stuff, it's always the same, until now.

Switching to a new language that actually rules it out does change it. I think that's a big deal. It's not just Android. I recently saw this headline. The Linux guy, Greg, number two as far as I know, said Rust will save Linux from AI. I saw that. I was like, I'm putting that quote in my talk right now. What he means is this. It's actually what I said. We're seeing more and more vulnerabilities. We need to have a systematic fix to prevent them. We can't get by on patching continuously. I do want to say, before I pivot a little bit, to say that for those of you who are saying, I use Java. It's fine. Or something, I don't have to worry about memory safety. That's true. You have other kinds of problems that need to be considered and taken care of. Rust luckily is young enough not to have our own Rust4Shell or whatever.

I'm sure we'll find some problems sooner or later. This is what I mean by, all of us need to reckon with every language, is how are we going to get to the highest levels of reliability as quickly as possible? Where that leaves me is I think when your whole point is being reliability, that's your pitch, you're well positioned here. When it comes down to, if coding is really cheap, then you should pick not based on what you have, not based on what you know, but based on what you want, your properties you want to have in the future. This is, I think, the big thing that is starting to shift in the way that our industry is approaching language choice, technology stack choice, and so on. Why not save money? That's the question I know a lot of us at Amazon are asking. Why not reduce exposure to vulnerabilities?

I gave you the hard sell. Rust and agents are good. Could they be better? I think so. Let me give you an example of what I mean. There's a library out there that was released pretty recently, it's called Toasty. It's an object relational mapper for Rust. It's a database interop library. It was written by Carl Lerche, if you know much about Rust. He's the creator of the Tokio project. He's a big deal. It's really cool. It lets you write these high-level programs that then will go into your database. You write very Rusty programs, and it goes into the database in an efficient way. It works by this concept called a derive, which is a macro in Rust that will auto-generate code, sort of like a decorator in Python, if you know that. You can add these annotations, like this is a unique field and whatnot.

This field is auto-generated and so on. Then when you do that, the derive will generate the glue code you need to work with your database. It works against SQL. It works against DynamoDB. It works against a bunch of stuff. You might have, it uses some of Rust macros. You say, I'm going to create an entry, create a new row. It looks natural, like a struct creation. You get helper methods saying, search by email or whatnot. It demonstrates some of what makes Rust really successful. It has these guardrails. When you have a custom function called get_by_email, you can't pass an integer as an email address, like you could if you were, say, doing string substitution or variables in SQL. It's well-typed and it's checked up front. It's also efficient. It generates code that understands the overall query you're trying to do and generates good code.

When I asked Claude about it, at least a couple weeks ago, Claude didn't even know that it existed. It said, what library do you recommend? It gave me a bunch of good suggestions, but none of them are Toasty, which is the new hotness, or at least from my point of view, looks pretty cool. Then I said, ok, Claude, how about if I tell you I want you to use Toasty, can you please make me a database as a sample application? You can even see my typo. I think that was supposed to be executable, not write me an execute. Claude figured that out. Claude goes off, and to its credit, goes and searches the web, finds stuff, reads documentation. It's a lot of tokens. It took it a lot of time. It wound up with something that runs. That's pretty cool. If you look closely, you start to notice a few things.

First of all, it's using Toasty 0.3. At that time, the most recent was 0.5. Now I think it's 0.7. It was using an old version. I've seen that actually quite a lot, that Claude likes to just pick whatever version out of the ether that it knows well. I think what it comes to is the world is moving a lot faster than it ever did. We're generating new software really fast. The training cycle is this slow-moving average of the web. It's not going to be able to keep up at the same pace. What we really want, I think, is some way to get ourselves involved and to help give an opinionated take on what the right thing is. I'll notice it was using an old version of a library. That's one thing. Also, it was using an old version of Rust, 3 years old, using Rust 2021, not Rust 2024.

Another thing I see even with the latest models all the time. The most frustrating thing from my point of view about all of this is that I can't help. I work on the Rust compiler. I work on the Rust programming language. I have no influence into what Claude Code is going to do when I ask it something, or Codex, or Gemini CLI, or OpenCode, you name it. These are all these vertical applications that aren't easily and readily extensible.

This is where this Symposium project comes in that I've been working on. I have a lot of ambitions, but my vision for Symposium is it's an agent-oriented tool chain. A tool chain is like your compiler, your package manager. I want one that is designed and geared to be used by agents, because I think that more and more, they're going to be the primary people running an actual compiler. It's a member of Rust Foundation's Innovation Lab. It's an open-source project, part of the Rust Foundation, right now mostly supported by me, but I'm hoping to build a proper project around it. The way it works is very simple. You write cargo install symposium. That's going to install the Symposium application. Then you run cargo agents init. This cargo agents is what I said I want like an agent-oriented tool chain. That's what I'm imagining is you'll write cargo agents, and there'll be various commands that are geared for and tailored for use by agents.

In the moment, you say init and you pick what agents are you planning to work with? Could be Claude Code, could be Codex, whatever. Check your boxes. We're going to go and configure things so that Symposium will be invoked as part of their lifecycle. The very first thing that's going to happen as a result is we're going to give general Rust guidance that is tailored to, like, for example, use Rust 2024, not Rust 2021. Always use cargo add, which will bring you the latest version of the crates. Always run cargo fmt. These things are very basic. Models aren't doing them right now. This is an interesting point. I assume this will change over time. At the moment, this steering is still needed. That's the basic level. The more interesting level is that we allow crate authors to write skills to guide the agent in how to use their crate.

This is trying to work around that problem of, I've introduced something new. The LLMs don't know about it yet. The world doesn't know about it yet. How can I have an agent actually make use of it? Maybe I can package up a skill that tells the agent how to use it and then have Symposium go and install it. You get to write a skill. You can put it in your crate. Then what Symposium will do is when it gets invoked as part of tool use or other hooks, it goes and checks what your dependencies are, checks against a set of databases, and just brings the skills into your directory so that they're available for your agent. That means instead of going off to search the web and burn tokens and come up with an old version of Toasty, you would just get the results right there.

It also has various APIs, like this one is one of my favorites, crate info. It's so simple. All it does is say, here's the source to this crate, which the way Cargo works is always available in a cache. That's really useful because without this, agents don't know what the API is a lot of the time. They'll just go hallucinate and it won't compile. Then they'll say, let me go mess around. Maybe they'll build the docs and try to parse the HTML, which is really inefficient. Just telling them, like, here's the source code. Go read it. At least what I found to be the best way is just give them the information they want. They're very good at grepping through source as it happens. The other nice thing, there's some subtle things when you build it in your tool chain. You can be sure that it's the exact version you're using as opposed to whatever version they found when they searched the web. As a side note, if the package isn't one that you're already using, we'll put it in a temporary directory and so forth. Always works.

These are some simple things. They get at a principle that I think is really important and really powerful, it's basically extensibility. In my mind, it's the reason that I like to work on developer tools, is that I think all of us have something unique to offer. Some kernel of great idea that we can bring in there and contribute to make something better. Or we have our own unique needs that nobody is necessarily going to tailor for us. I really like environments that can be adjusted and played with and become a playground. I loved Emacs back in the day. I love VS Code. I don't love this about agents. It's nice that we have marketplaces and so on, but they don't have as much power as I would like. I really want to release that flourish of creativity. Rust embodies this with I showed you the procedural macros.

We have a small standard library on purpose so that people write libraries out in the open and we get to have the best of whatever they're using. I think this is a really powerful philosophy. Let me tell you a little bit about how it works in more detail. Right now, the way we have it is there's a centralized repository called recommendations. In there, if I am the author of the Toasty crate, the crate I mentioned earlier, I can do a couple things. One of them is I can add a PR with adding a plugin like this. I make a directory. My plugin is called SYMPOSIUM.toml. It will say, I'm making a plugin named Toasty. It should be triggered whenever the user depends on the Toasty crate. It brings these skills available which you can find in the same directory like this create-model skill.

That's one way to go. That's not my preferred way, but it's a convenient way. Let me show you the other way and then I'll explain what the tradeoffs are. There's another way, which is you can actually put the skill in your crate file itself. A crate in Rust is just a library. It packages up the source code, but it can also package up other auxiliary files like skills. In that way, I still make a file in the central repo to say this is a place that Symposium should look. There's no coordination needed. At the moment, we are still requiring this centralized file. I'll explain why. It gives you a clue there. The previous one, this one where everything is in one repo, this is useful, sort of like TypeScript in the beginning, if you recall. I think they still do. In the same way, I want to be able to add skills to existing crates that don't have them already. You can add it on the side, or better yet, if you're in control, you can put it inside. I mentioned that we are still requiring something in the central repo. That's because there's pretty obviously a security concern here. I don't actually think it's a new one.

Which is to say, when you bring in something from your dependency and you let it give guidance to your agent, it could tell your agent to do a lot of things. I don't think it's new. It's not just skills. I talked a lot about skills. We also bridge up things like MCP servers. If someone's depending on your crate, maybe you have an MCP server that gives access to some of the data. I'll talk about some interesting use cases later. Same with hooks. You can install hooks. You can configure all the things that agents give you to configure so that you can get into the development experience. Now, if I zoom out a little bit, though, this means if I'm using a crate, my agent knows how to use it. There's still another interesting question. How does my agent know which crates to use in the first place?

How do you know? When I talk to people who are adopting Rust, actually, learning the language isn't usually their biggest problem. How do I know which ones are the right ones to use? What are the tradeoffs between them? That can be a very difficult choice. It's the flip side. I'm super into extensibility, but also, when you give everyone the power to build things, suddenly you have to pick from a lot of different choices, and that's debilitating in its own way. What we're trying to do with Symposium is partner with another project that I think is like the other half to address this aspect of using Rust experience. We have this other project called battery packs, and I'll explain what a battery pack is.

The short version is it's like a best practice guidance. Symposium will steer your agent towards, you should go check out these battery packs. These are actually pretty vetted, highly recommended sets of libraries. A battery pack is a special crate, which doesn't really have source code. It just has a list of other crates that you might want to use for a purpose, like a network service or something else. It has documentation that's cross-cutting, because sometimes there's docs that don't belong in any one thing. It's not about, how do I use this library? It's about, how do I use these two libraries together to do something different? Of course, it can package up skills. Actually, any of the extensions I talked about, MCP servers. It's just a full-on Symposium plugin source. One example of what we're expecting to do, I mean, I work at Amazon, so network services are always top of mind.

We're working towards having an opinionated network service pack that has, here's all the pieces you need to put together, and that includes things like a profiling engine, the tools to run a profiler. Also, I know there's people with specialized needs, like a small embedded environment, maybe a battery pack for some sensor node architecture. I also want mainstream ones. We're spinning up this Rust commercial network in the foundation, and the idea is to bring together industrial users of Rust, have them say, here's the libraries we're using in production. What the Agent Client Protocol is, is it reimagines how agents and clients or users interact. Today's model is like this. You have the user, they're typing over on their keyboard, and they're running a program, like a CLI or a GUI. That program is talking to the agent and managing that whole communication. With ACP, you switch it out. The user picks a frontend tool, a CLI or a GUI, but it doesn't specify what agent it works with. Instead, it uses a JSON RPC protocol to say, I'm here, I'm starting a new session. The user typed hello, what would you like to say back, and so on. In many cases now, more and more, it's native support. Especially from agents that are trying to get a foothold, this is like a sensible thing to do, because if they offer ACP, then anyone using an ACP client can use them more easily. It's a nice way to get a foothold and separate concerns. They may not have to make a GUI anymore because now there are canned GUIs they can reuse. On the flip side, you have a bunch of editors, so Zed, but also all the IntelliJ family ones.

This gets us to the latest thing that I've been trying to do with ACP and how this connects to extensibility. So far, we've seen that if you put an interface in between a client and an agent, you can have novel kinds of clients or novel kinds of agents. Side note, how many of you remember ELIZA? I wrote an ELIZA ACP, which I think is great. ELIZA is just like a hacky regex that really feels like you're talking to a therapist, even though it's not. 1970s AI resurgence. Here's me saying, use Zed, or IntelliJ. They're really good. Plus, they use ACP. Everybody wins. I'm expecting that we will see more things like this, whether it's ACP or something else.

As agentic coding becomes more mainstream, we're going to need to have some standards that let us build on top of it and build more complex workflows. One of the places we're seeing a lot of interest, actually, is in enterprise applications and so on, where they want to build integrations for their employees to offer a better experience than just a CLI.

You should use Rust for your next project, especially if you're using AI. If you've tried it and bounced, give it another try because it feels different now. Second, when you do it, use Symposium, cargo agents init. Easy. Third, portability sucks, but I hope it will get better.

#9928. Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as

In theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:

The following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError), which will trigger a panic when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

You might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this is the common case.

I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she works on lend themselves more towards these issues compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t ready to kill my darlings.1 Skip to the next section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

In Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex2 system call. It allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three unique values:

Flow chart showing how a mutex acquisition is implemented in Rust, using atomic operations and futex primitives. Note how the uncontended case remains entirely in user-space and does not sleep the thread.

Rust implements this with a few atomic operations and the futex_wait call. Crucially, the path for locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that requires a context switch is futex_wait.

Unlocking is even simpler. The thread that holds the mutex first releases the lock, then optionally, if there was an indication that the lock was contended, wakes any sleeping threads so they can try to acquire the lock.

Flow chart showing how a mutex release in Rust. First, we swap the current value with 0, and depending on whether it was originally 1 (simply locked) or 2 (contended), we optionally wake any sleeping threads.

As discussed in too much detail above, (un)locking mutexes is cheap as long as they’re not contended, and when contended, they are at least cheap instruction wise. This is where poisoning mutexes get you.

In short, being able to poison is a cost that is always paid, but seldom used. To start, poisoning is essentially implemented by adding an AtomicBool field to every Mutex. Due to alignment, this grows the size of every mutex by anywhere from zero bytes to an additional pointer. This isn’t terrible but for use cases where you have many mutexes guarding small objects, this can add up.

The real issue to me however is in code size. Let’s start with another contrived example, a function that reads its argument, copies it, and returns it. An idealised version of that would be the following.

This compiles down to 2 instructions and a label. Copy the data into the register then return.

Of course, this doesn’t work for any context that needs shared mutation, but we can consider it our baseline. Perfection would look like this. So, let’s ignore that atomic integers exist and add a mutex to this story. We will go over the generated assembly code for each, and you can compare the code in its entirety in this Compiler Explorer overview.

We can update the code above to actually use mutexes, and simply lock-then-unwrap the mutex.

This compiles to a total of 147 lines of assembly which I’m not going to reproduce here in full.

To divide that up a different way, we have

Most of this is inlined into the function. This in turn affects performance, as this limits how much of your “real” code fits in the CPU’s instruction cache. The laptop I’m writing this on has a paltry 32KiB of instruction cache. Luckily we can do better.

Most of the code generated in the previous example had to do with setting up the panic, and checking the conditions. But we don’t care about panicking. We can simply acknowledge the PoisonError and continue. That looks as follows:

This results in only 68 lines of assembly, which is much better, though all of it is inlined to our function. Compared to before, we’ve lost all panic related code. There’s still some unnecessary branching related to whether the mutex is poisoned, as well as a little dance to track poisoning in our function. Our function can never panic, but compiler optimisations currently do not remove the atomic loads and stores involved here. Nevertheless, if you want to target stable Rust and you don’t care about panics, this is what you should do at the moment.

In the current nightly builds of Rust, there are non-poisoning mutexes that can don’t have any of the overhead. We can optimise our code from above to make use of them.

No unwrapping, and it only results in 34 lines of assembly code. This is short enough for me to walk through it.

I’ve added comments and labels to the assembly so the steps from the (un)locking flow charts become visible. As far as assembly code goes, it’s very readable and simple. Which, of course, is exactly what you want from fundamental library code.

The additional logic checking the poison state, adding a destructor for the mutex guard, and, if you choose ergonomics, even panic machinery, significantly bloats the code of a rather fundamental operation.

Besides the purely technical argument that poisoning makes all code larger and slower than it needs to be, there is a different one. As discussed previously, code that doesn’t care about mutex poisoning should generally write:

It’s reasonably efficient and available on stable Rust. But that whole unwrap_or_else part takes up more than half the line. No worry, you might say, we can make it shorter:

This works well enough. It’s less efficient than the previous example, but it’s nice and short. If your code never panics, it’s even perfectly safe. You might have spotted a load-bearing “if” already. It’s kind of hard to guarantee your code does not panic. Array indexing, integer division, and a whole host of other features might panic unexpectedly.

This is hard for experienced developers, but for those learning it’s even worse. It also trains bad habits. Every time a beginner Rust developer writes unwrap() instead of handling their errors, a puppy steps on a Lego brick. Or causes a widespread internet outage. One of the two, I forget which.

We should not want to include APIs into the standard library that return a Result that is “expected” to be unwrapped. Infallible operations should not fail.

Poisoning protects against a task panicking in the middle of an invariant violation. But why must this be specific to mutexes? The example from before works just as well with a simple mutable borrow. Panics may still happen, and you may still catch them.

This is actually a fairly common problem. In a more recent blog post, researchers at Microsoft highlight various places they’ve found where even the standard library gets this wrong.

In most cases however, this is fine, as it is with the mutex example given in the beginning. You don’t need to poison this reference. But for applications where you do, it’s kinda nice to be able to.

It’s not hard to imagine a wrapper that adds poisoning behaviour when you want to have it. Crucially, this needs to be an additive wrapper. You can add a poisoning system to something. You cannot strip out the poisoning system from a primitive that has it. Poison safety is important for the specific use cases that need it, but most do not.

I don’t believe it’s worth it to saddle mutexes in particular with this overhead when the problem is near universal with any mutable state. State invariants are just hard that way.

One might draw a comparison between poison safety and buffer safety. In Rust, we always do bounds checking, relying on the compiler to optimise it out in cases it can be proven redundant. Can’t poison safety be the same? And the answer, it turns out, is no.

The compiler cannot optimise poisoning away. It requires any mutex carry additional data to track it. Maybe the compiler can figure out one particular critical section cannot panic, and therefore it can leave out the setup and clean-up, but in general it cannot avoid checking the state. This is overhead that always applies, and hurts, especially in environments where code size is more restricted.

In C++, there are a few choices in the standard that make certain containers less efficient than they could be4. Because of how standardisation works, the containers can never be “fixed”. This causes third party implementations, such as Abseil and Boost, to become the de facto standard.

Mutexes in Rust suffer from the same problem. The standard library has poisoning, but people don’t want poisoning, so instead they opt for crates like parking_lot. I believe this is bad for the ecosystem as a whole. When the standard library offers a feature, it should be an uncontroversially good choice, unless you are doing something hyper specific. We don’t have to be “batteries included” but the parts that are there should be a good fit.

I started out writing this blog in response to a movement to change the default mutex behaviour in Rust. It seems to me there are three camps:

Rain’s blog argued for option 1. I believe we both agree that option 2 is a terrible idea. I think we should do at least option 3. Option 4 would be a good edition improvement, but it is also a significant compatibility issue, and even I find it hard to argue that it’s really worth it.

Which is a roundabout way of saying that we really should stabilise std::sync::nonpoison and definitely should not make std::sync::Mutex panic by default.

For various reasons, this article took me about a year to write. Not everything is still relevant, or as cohesive as I’d like. I’m publishing mainly for my own sanity. I do still hope that the mutex discussion around stabilising the new mutexes ends up in a good place.

Matt Godbolt’s compiler explorer has been an invaluable help in writing this blog, as has Rain’s original blog on the discussion.

Cover image Red fly agaric mushrooms in grass by Pixabay user Sven Kirsch.

It is becoming apparent to me that I just like explaining mutexes and I don’t know what to do about that. ↩︎

Fast Userspace muTEX. See futex(2) for more on the system call and futex(7) for its semantics ↩︎

For generic definitions (e.g. Mutex) the compiler must generate code for every unique T that gets used, and for loads of reasons often more than once per T. The compiler development docs have a deeper explanation of monomorphisation. ↩︎

A famous example is std::unordered_map, which suffers from being over-specified and that prevents more efficient implementations. ↩︎

My name is Bert Peters and I'm a software developer/computer enthusiast/nerd. I write articles and create demos about technology and miscellaneous items that strike my fancy, and I fail to hide my love for Rust.

#9927. CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

New questionnaire captures critical data and information that improves the agency’s ability to assess incidents, identify trends and prioritize response actions.

WASHINGTON — Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.

The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in Two Days

“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”

While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.

For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questionsweb page.

As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.

#9926. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.
