#9836. Small Language Models, Not Giant LLMs, Should Power the Next Generation of AI Agents

Source: arXiv:2506.02153, available under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Large language models (LLMs) are often praised for exhibiting near-human performance on a wide range of tasks and valued for their ability to hold a general conversation. The rise of agentic AI systems is, however, ushering in a mass of applications in which language models perform a small number of specialized tasks repetitively and with little variation.

Here we lay out the position that small language models (SLMs) are sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems, and are therefore the future of agentic AI. Our argumentation is grounded in the current level of capabilities exhibited by SLMs, the common architectures of agentic systems, and the economy of LM deployment. We further argue that in situations where general-purpose conversational abilities are essential, heterogeneous agentic systems (i.e., agents invoking multiple different models) are the natural choice. We discuss the potential barriers for the adoption of SLMs in agentic systems and outline a general LLM-to-SLM agent conversion algorithm.

Our position (The views and positions expressed in this paper are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of any entities they represent.), formulated as a value statement, highlights the significance of the operational and economic impact even a partial shift from LLMs to SLMs is to have on the AI agent industry. We aim to stimulate the discussion on the effective use of AI resources and hope to advance the efforts to lower the costs of AI of the present day. Calling for both contributions to and critique of our position, we commit to publishing all such correspondence at research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/slm-agents.

The deployment of agentic artificial intelligence is on a meteoric rise. Recent surveys show that more than a half of large IT enterprises are actively using AI agents, with 21% having adopted just within the last year [14]. Aside from the users, markets also see substantial economic value in AI agents: As of late 2024, the agentic AI sector had seen more than USD 2bn in startup funding, was valued at USD 5.2bn, and was expected to grow to nearly USD 200bn by 2034 [46, 51]. Put plainly, there is a growing expectation that AI agents will play a substantial role in the modern economy.

The core components powering most modern AI agents are (very) large language models [52, 48]. It is the LLMs that provide the foundational intelligence that enables agents to make strategic decisions about when and how to use available tools, control the flow of operations needed to complete tasks, and, if necessary, to break down complex tasks into manageable subtasks and to perform reasoning for action planning and problem-solving [52, 17]. A typical AI agent then simply communicates with a chosen LLM API endpoint by making requests to centralized cloud infrastructure that hosts these models [52].

LLM API endpoints are specifically designed to serve a large volume of diverse requests using one generalist LLM. This operational model is deeply ingrained in the industry. In fact, it forms the foundation of substantial capital investment in the hosting cloud infrastructure – estimated at USD 57bn [16]. It is anticipated that this operational model will remain the cornerstone of the industry and that the large initial investment will deliver returns comparable to traditional software and internet solutions within 3-4 years [57].

In this work, we recognize the dominance of the standard operational model but verbally challenge one of its aspects, namely the custom that the agents’ requests to access language intelligence are – in spite of their comparative simplicity – handled by singleton choices of generalist LLMs. We state (Section 2), argue (Section 3), and defend (Section 4) the position that the small, rather than large, language models are the future of agentic AI. We, however, recognize the business commitment and the now-legacy praxis that is the cause for the contrary state of the present (Section 5). In remedy, we provide an outline of a conversion algorithm for the migration of agentic applications from LLMs to SLMs (Section 6), and call for a wider discussion (Section 7). If needed to concretize our stance, we attach a set of short case studies estimating the potential extent of LLM-to-SLM replacement in selected popular open-source agents (Appendix B).

For the purpose of concretizing our position, we use the following working definitions:

We justify the wording of these definitions in Appendix A, but note that their choice has little bearing on the essence of our position. We note that as of 2025, we would be comfortable with considering most models below 10bn parameters in size to be SLMs.

We use the words agent and agentic system interchangeably, preferring the former when emphasizing the software with some agency as a whole (e.g., “as seen in popular coding agents”) and the latter when highlighting the systems aspect of the agentic application as a sum of its components (e.g., “not all LMs of an agentic system are replaceable by SLMs”). For brevity, we focus on LMs as the bedrock of agentic applications and do not explicitly consider vision-language models, although we note that our position and most of our arguments readily extend to vision-language models as well.

V1 principally sufficiently powerful to handle language modeling errands of agentic applications;

V2 inherently more operationally suitable for use in agentic systems than LLMs;

V3 necessarily more economical for the vast majority of LM uses in agentic systems than their general-purpose LLM counterparts by the virtue of their smaller size;

and that on the basis of items V1, V2 and V3 SLMs are the future of agentic AI.

The phrasing of our position is deliberate. In its statement, we wish to convey that the described future development is ultimately a necessary consequence of the differences between SLMs and LLMs if the natural priorities are followed. We do not make a recommendation or try to impose an obligation — we make a statement of what we see as a faithful reflection of the community’s values in this context.

We assert that the dominance of LLMs in the design of AI agents is both excessive and misaligned with the functional demands of most agentic use cases. While LLMs offer impressive generality and conversational fluency, the majority of agentic sub tasks in deployed agentic systems are repetitive, scoped, and non-conversational—calling for models that are efficient, predictable, and inexpensive. In this context, SLMs not only suffice, but are often preferable. They offer several advantages: lower latency, reduced memory and computational requirements, and significantly lower operational costs, all while maintaining adequate task performance in constrained domains.

Our position stems from a pragmatic view of language model usage patterns within agentic architectures. These systems typically decompose complex goals into modular sub-tasks, each of which can be reliably handled by specialized or fine-tuned SLMs. We argue that insisting on LLMs for all such tasks reflects a misallocation of computational resources—one that is economically inefficient and environmentally unsustainable at scale.

Moreover, in cases where general reasoning or open-domain dialogue is essential, we advocate for heterogeneous agentic systems, where SLMs are used by default and LLMs are invoked selectively and sparingly. This modular composition — combining the precision and efficiency of SLMs with the generality of LLMs — enables the construction of agents that are both cost-effective and capable.

Ultimately, we observe that shifting the paradigm from LLM-centric to SLM-first architectures represents to many not only a technical refinement but also a Humean moral ought. As the AI community grapples with rising infrastructure costs and environmental concerns, adopting and normalizing the use of SLMs in agentic workflows can play a crucial role in promoting responsible and sustainable AI deployment.

We support items V1, V2 and V3 by the following non-exclusive arguments.

A1 SLMs are sufficiently powerful to take the place of LLMs in agentic systems. This argument stands in support of item V1.

Over the past few years, the capabilities of small language models have advanced significantly. Although the LM scaling laws remain observed, the scaling curve between model size and capabilities is becoming increasingly steeper, implying that the capabilities of newer small language models are much closer to those of previous large language models. Indeed, recent advances show that well-designed small language models can meet or exceed the task performance previously attributed only to much larger models.

Extensive comparisons with large models have been conducted in the individual works cited below, but not all capabilities assessed by benchmarks are essential to their deployment in the agentic context. Here we highlight their aptitude for commonsense reasoning (an indicator of basic understanding), tool calling and code generation (both indicators of the ability to correctly communicate across the model→tool/code interface; see Figure 1; [77, 78]), and instruction following (ability to correctly respond back across the code←model interface; [83]). In each case, we also quote the efficiency increase if stated by the authors.

Note that on top of competitive off-the-shelf performance, the reasoning capabilities of SLMs can be enhanced by light-weight selective finetuning [45] or at inference time with self-consistency, verifier feedback, or tool augmentation — e.g., Toolformer (6.7bn) outperforms GPT-3 (175bn) via API use [65], and appropriately prompted language models rival directly applied LLMs on math problems [84].

In sum, with modern training, prompting, and agentic augmentation techniques, capability — not the parameter count — is the binding constraint. SLMs now supply sufficient reasoning power for a substantial portion of agentic invocations, making them not just viable, but comparatively more suitable than LLMs for modular and scalable agentic systems.

A2 SLMs are more economical than LLMs in agentic systems. This argument supports item V3.

Small models provide significant benefits in cost-efficiency, adaptability, and deployment flexibility. These advantages are specifically valuable in agentic workflows where specialization and iterative refinement are critical. Section 3.1 detailed a number of efficiency comparisons of the listed SLMs to relevant LLMs. Here we draw a more encompassing picture to support item A2.

Modular system design. The position outlined in [56] presents a thorough argument in favor of composite agentic systems. Here we note that the approach of leveraging several models of varying sizes aligns well with the real-world heterogeneity of agentic tasks and is already slowly being incorporated into major software development frameworks [28]. Furthermore, this newly discovered sense for modularity in the context of agents allows for the easy addition of new skills and the ability to adapt to changing requirements, and is consistent with the push for modularity in language model design [27, 12, 40].

The above-mentioned “Lego-like” composition of agentic intelligence—scaling out by adding small, specialized experts instead of scaling up monolithic models—yields systems that are cheaper, faster to debug, easier to deploy, and better aligned with the operational diversity of real-world agents. When combined with tool calling, caching, and fine-grained routing, SLM-first architectures appear to offer the best path forward for cost-effective, modular, and sustainable agentic AI.

A3 SLMs possess greater operational flexibility in comparison to LLMs. This argument stands in support of items V2 and V3.

Due to their small size and the associated reduction in pre-training and fine-tuning costs (Section 3.2), SLMs are inherently more flexible than their large counterparts when appearing in agentic systems. As such, it becomes much more affordable and practical to train, adapt, and deploy multiple specialized expert models for different agentic routines. This efficiency enables rapid iteration and adaptation, making it feasible to address evolving user needs, including supporting new behaviors, meeting new output formatting requirements, and complying with changing local regulation in selected markets [73, 41, 72].

One particularly notable and desirable consequence of SLM flexibility when put in place of LLMs is the ensuing democratization of agents. When more individuals and organizations can participate in developing language models with the aim for deployment in agentic systems, the aggregate population of agents is more likely to represent a more diverse range of perspectives and societal needs. This diversity can then help with reducing the risk of systemic biases and encourage competition and innovation. With more actors entering the field to create and refine models, the field will advance more rapidly [38].

A4 Agentic applications are interfaces to a limited subset of LM capabilities. This supports items V1 and V2.

An AI agent is essentially a heavily instructed and externally choreographed gateway to a language model featuring a human-computer interface and a selection of tools that, when engaged correctly, do something of utility [73]. From this perspective, the underlying large language model that was engineered to be a powerful generalist is through a set of tediously written prompts and meticulously orchestrated context management restricted to operate within a small section of its otherwise large pallet of skills. Thus, we argue that a SLM appropriately fine-tuned for the selected prompts would suffice while having the above-mentioned benefits of increased efficiency and greater flexibility.

It could be argued back that the careful interfacing with a generalist LLM is necessary for strong performance on the narrow task because of the LLM’s better understanding of the broader language and the world (item AV1). This is addressed in Section 4.1.

A5 Agentic interactions necessitate close behavioral alignment. This aligns with item V2.

A typical AI agent has frequent interactions with code, be it through LM tool calling or by returning output that is to be parsed by a piece of agentic code that makes the LM call [52]. It is essential for the success of these interactions that the generated tool call and the generated output conform to strict formatting requirements imposed on it by the order, typing, and nature of the tool’s parameters, and the expectation of the code invoking the LM, respectively. In such cases, it becomes unnecessary for the model to handle multiple different formats (e.g. JSON/XML/Python for tool calls and XML/YAML/Markdown/Latex for output [54]), as only one would be chosen for consistency across the agentic application. It is also undesirable for the model to make the occasional hallucinatory mistake and respond in a format different from that being expected by the “code parts” of the agentic system. It is because of this that the SLM trained with a single formatting decision enforced during its post-training or encouraged through additional fine-tuning at a low cost is preferable over a general-purpose LLM in the context of AI agents.

A6 Agentic systems naturally allow for heterogeneity in the selection of models that they use. This aligns with item V2.

A language model can itself be a tool called by another language model. Likewise, every time the agent’s code invokes a language model, it can, in principle, choose any language model. This is illustrated in Figure 1. We argue that incorporating multiple language models of different sizes and capabilities for queries or operations of different levels of complexity offers a natural way for the introduction of SLMs. In the context of Figure 1- Left, an LLM can be used for the model with the root agency, while a SLM could be used for the subordinate LM. In Figure 1- Right, all LMs could in principle be specialized SLMs: one for conversationality, another one for carrying out controller-defined language modeling tasks.

A7 Agentic interactions are a good source for data for future model improvement. This is fundamentally supportive of item V2.

As noted in Section 3.4, invocations of tools and language models during an agentic process are often accompanied by careful prompting that focuses the language model on delivering the narrow functionality that is required at the time. Each one of these invocations is itself a natural source of data for future improvement (under the necessary assumption that no non-retainable confidential data is being processed). A listener decorating the tool/model call interface can gather specialized instruction data that can later be used to produce a fine-tune an expert SLM and lower the cost of that call in the future (see logger in Figure 1). We argue that this avenue is enabled by the architecture of agents [52] and produces high-quality organic data (that can be further post-filtered by considering the overall success of the workflow), thus making the production of expert SLMs to stand in place of LLMs a natural step in agent deployment — not just an auxiliary effort.

The following significant alternative views have been expressed in the academic and popular literature.

AV1 Let T be a single task using general language and let L,S be a large and a small language model of the same generation, respectively. The performance of L on T will always trump that of S.

This alternative view disputes item V2 and rests on the following counter-arguments:

CA1 There is a non-negligible body of empirical evidence of the superiority of large language models in general language understanding over small language models of the same generation. LLMs acquire their language understanding capabilities in accordance with scaling laws [18]. Their larger scale then enables them to demonstrate better performance across a wide array of specialized natural language tasks, including text generation, translation, and reasoning, outperforming small models trained both (a) in the same general fashion and (b) from scratch specifically for these tasks [58]. It can then be said that to claim otherwise is to contradict the LM scaling laws [32, 31].

CA2 Moreover, recent studies also purport that LLMs possess a “semantic hub” mechanism, which has been hypothesized to enable them to integrate and abstract semantic information from various modalities and languages in a generalized manner [80]. If true, LLMs could be thought to generalize knowledge across languages and domains far more effectively than smaller models, which under the same study lack the capacity for the presence of such a hub [80]. It can then argued that while small language models may be efficient for narrowly defined or highly specialized tasks, their limited scale fundamentally restricts their ability to achieve the same level of general language understanding in these specialized as LLMs because of the lack of room for the internalization of complex abstractions.

A conclusion can be then drawn that LLM generalist models will always retain the advantage of universally better performance on language tasks, no matter how narrowly defined, over small language models of the same generation. This to be to their advantage over SLMs when deployed in agentic applications.

The above alternative view is the most popularly cited belief against the use of SLMs, even when only a narrow language task needs to be performed [2, 71, 30, 1].

We believe that item CA1 is too limited to attack item V2, namely because

A8 Popular scaling law studies assume the model architecture to be kept constant [32, 31] within the same generation, whereas the recent work on small language model training demonstrates that there are distinct performance benefits to considering different architectures for different model sizes [23, 9].

A9 The flexibility of small language models (Section 3.3) comes to the rescue. A small language model can be easily fine-tuned for the task T of item AV1 to perform to the desired level of reliability. This is unaccounted for in scaling law studies.

A10 Reasoning (or, more generally, test-time compute scaling; see Section 3.2) is significantly more affordable. A small language model, still retaining its benefits of greater cross-device agility can be reasonable expected to be scalable at inference time to the desired level of reliability.

We also believe that item CA2 is too arcane to attack item V2 because

A11 The utility of the purported “semantic hub” shows itself when tasks or inputs at hand to be processed by the LM are complex. However, advanced agentic systems are either designed in their entirety or at least actively prompted to perform decompositions of complex problems and inputs [52, 17]. Therefore, we argue to the contrary that invocations of small language models within agentic systems would be on appropriately broken-down into sub-tasks so simple that any general abstract understanding due to the hub would be of little utility.

AV2 The per-token inference cost benefit of the smallness of specialized SLMs in agentic applications is dwarfed by the economy of scale.

It could be argued that the analysis in item A2 that put forth in favor of item V3 was ignorant of the wider business of AI model deployment:

CA3 It is more difficult to fully utilize and properly balance the load for an expert SLM inference endpoint than it is for a generalist LLM endpoint [70, 25].

CA4 The costs of inference infrastructure setup combined with the costs of acquiring and retaining talent for its upkeep are often omitted in inference cost calculations but figure more prominently if the deployment of (S)LMs became the responsibility of the agent service developer. Early industrial reports point to considerable costs associated with these operations [39, 13, 67].

Acknowledgment. We acknowledge that item AV2 is a valid view, with the exact economical considerations being highly case-specific. We believe that the jury is still out on item AV2, but that several factors hint that item V3 might prevail:

A12 Recent improvements in inference scheduling and large inference system modularization offer unprecedented levels of inference system flexibility in monolithic computing clusters [85, 60, 50], countering the traditional stance expressed in item CA3.

A13 The most recent analyses on the set-up costs of inference infrastructure indicate a consistent falling trend due to underlying technological reasons [82, 4].

AV3 Both the agentic world utilizing SLMs and agentic world utilizing LLMs are equally possible worlds, but the “LLM agentic world” has a considerable head start in terms of deployment practice and optimization, and the industry inertia already funnels efforts into innovation solely in that direction.

Acknowledgment. We acknowledge item AV3 as a distinct possibility, but maintain the position that the weight of advantages described across items A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 and A7 can plausibily overturn the present state of affairs.

It would be prudent to ask oneself: If the items A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6 and A7 are truly compelling, why do the ever newer generations of agents seemingly just perpetuate the status quo of using generalist LLMs?

We believe the following to be among the today’s main barriers to wide-spread adoption of SLMs:

B1 Large amounts of upfront investment in centralized LLM inference infrastructure. As detailed in Section 1, large capital bets have been made on the centralized LLM inference being the leading paradigm in providing AI services in the future. As such, the industry has been much quicker at building the tools and infrastructure to that end, omitting any considerations for the possibility that more decentralized SLM or on-device inference might be equally feasible in the near future.

B2 Use of generalist benchmarks in SLM training, design, and evaluation. It must be pointed out that much of the work on SLM design and development follows the tracks of LLM design, focusing on the same generalist benchmarks in their development [47, 61]. On this point, [23] notes that if one focuses solely on benchmarks measuring the agentic utility of agents, the studied SLMs easily outperform larger models.

B3 Lack of popular awareness. SLMs often do not receive the level of marketing intensity and press attention LLMs do, despite their better suitability in many industrial scenarios.

We note that items B1, B2 and B3 are practical hurdles and far from being fundamental flaws of the SLM technology in the context of agentic AI. With advanced inference scheduling systems such as Dynamo [24], item B1 is being reduced to a mere effect of inertia. item B2 is becoming increasingly recognized in the field [23, 37], and it would be natural for item B3 to fall once the economic benefits of SLM deployment in agentic applications (item A2) are better known. With the inertia of item B1 in particular, we do not endeavor to give a timeline for the retreat of these barriers or the popular adoption of SLMs.

The very nature of agentic applications enables them to eventually switch from using LLM generalists to using SLM specialists at many of their interfaces. In the following steps, we outline an algorithm that describes one possible way to carry out the change of the underlying model painlessly.

S1 Secure usage data collection. The initial step involves deploying instrumentation to log all non-HCI agent calls, capturing input prompts, output responses, contents of individual tool calls, and optionally latency metrics for a later targeted optimization. In terms of implementation, it is the recommended practice to set up encrypted logging pipelines with role-based access controls [55] and anonymize all data with respect to its origins before storage [74]. See logger in Figure 1 for an illustration.

S2 Data curation and filtering. Begin collecting data through the pipelines of item S1. Once a satisfactory amount of data has been collected (10k-100k examples being sufficient for fine-tuning of small models as a rule of thumb [5, 22]), it is necessary to remove any PII, PHI, or any other application-specific sensitive data that could cause a data leak across user accounts once used to produce a SLM specialist. Many typical varieties of sensitive data can be detected and masked or removed using popular automated tools for dataset preparation [64, 62]. Application specific inputs (e.g. legal or internal documents) can be often be automatically paraphrased to obfuscate named entities and numerical details without compromising the general information content [11, 79, 76].

S3 Task clustering. Employ unsupervised clustering techniques on the collected prompts and agent actions to identify recurring patterns of requests or internal agent operations [35, 42, 21]. These clusters help define candidate tasks for SLM specialization. The granularity of tasks will depend on the diversity of operations; common examples include intent recognition, data extraction, summarization of specific document types, or code generation with respect to tools available to the agent.

S4 SLM selection. For each identified task, select one or more candidate SLMs. Criteria for selection include the SLM’s inherent capabilities (e.g., instruction following, reasoning, context window size), its performance on relevant benchmarks for the task type, its licensing, and its deployment footprint (memory, computational requirements). Models of Section 3.2 serve as good starting candidates.

S5 Specialized SLM fine-tuning. For each selected task and corresponding SLM candidate, prepare a task-specific dataset from the curated data collected in items S2 and S3. Then, fine-tune the chosen SLMs on these specialized datasets. PEFT techniques such as LoRA [34] or QLoRA [20] can be leveraged to reduce computational costs and memory requirements associated with fine-tuning, making the process more accessible. Full fine-tuning can also be considered if resources permit and maximal adaptation is required. In some cases, it may be beneficial to use knowledge distillation, where the specialist SLM is trained to mimic the outputs of the more powerful generalist LLM on the task-specific dataset. This can help transfer some of the more nuanced capabilities of the LLM to the SLM.

S6 Iteration and refinement. One may retrain the SLMs and the router model periodically with new data to maintain performance and adapt to evolving usage patterns. This forms a continuous improvement loop, returning to item S2 or item S4 as appropriate.

The agentic AI industry is showing the signs of a promise to have a transformative effect on white collar work and beyond.

It is the view of the authors that any expense savings or improvements on the sustainability of AI infrastructure would act as a catalyst for this transformation, and that it is thus eminently desirable to explore all options for doing so.

We therefore call for both contributions to and critique of our position, to be directed to agents@nvidia.com, and commit to publishing all such correspondence at research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/slm-agents.

This appendix provides two justifications for the choice of definitions in Section 2.1.

It is desirable to have a definition of SLMs that meets three key criteria:

We find item WD1 to possess all three. Item WD2 is then phrased to complement the set of all language models.

To explore the distinction between small and large language models in the context of agentic AI, let us adopt the uncompromising lens of an extremalist, for whom intelligence must be either maximally small or maximally large.

Imagine a super-intelligent system spanning galactic scales, marshaling all available matter to optimize its computations. Such a system, while theoretically capable of addressing profound questions would face insurmountable physical constraints. The speed of light limits communication, with round-trip delays across a galaxy potentially spanning tens of thousands of years [63]. This latency precludes real-time coordination, fragmenting the system into loosely coupled components rather than a unified "mind". At cosmological scales, spanning millions or billions of light-years, communication delays could approach or exceed the universe’s age of 13.8 billion years [15]. Such a system, while vast, would be impractical for human-relevant applications, its computations unfolding over eons.

Conversely, consider an infinitely small intelligent system, reduced to the minimal substrate capable of computation. Such a system, akin to the simplest biological organisms, would lack the sensors, effectors, or computational capacity to meaningfully interact with its environment. Its intelligence would be constrained to rudimentary evolution, much like early life forms that emerged 3.5 billion years ago [66]. Yet, even in nature, scale varies dramatically: living organisms range from bacteria (hundreds of nanometers) to blue whales (up to 30 meters), the heaviest ones being limited by heat dissipation due to their high volume-to-surface ratio [26]. At the cosmic scale, all terrestrial life appears microscopic, suggesting that absolute size is less critical than functional adaptability.

Hereby: Humans, often regarded as a pinnacle of intelligence, offer a useful anchor for defining SLMs and LLMs. With a brain-to-body mass ratio surpassed only by small mammals like mice [49], humans balance computational efficiency with practical embodiment. SLMs, by analogy, are systems compact enough to run on personal devices, be trained with modest human interaction, or perform constrained, verifiable tasks. LLMs, in contrast, demand datacenter-scale infrastructure, organization-level training, and extensive validation, reflecting their computational load. The extremalist perspective hints at a profound truth: intelligence is not defined by size alone but by the balance of capability, efficiency, and context. For agentic workflows, SLMs may offer agility and accessibility, while LLMs provide depth at the cost of scale.

It is because of this apparent continuum that, if pressed to provide a definition of SLMs, we choose to anchor it in characteristics of a model that can be deployed in a distributed fashion with present-day technology and be interactive enough when engaging with a human to be of utility. Proceeding in such a way, the contemporary instances of the definition will evolve as the technology underpinning these models advances, making the definition sufficiently timeless to be practical.

This appendix assesses the potential extent of replacing large language model invocations with small language models in three popular open-source agents: MetaGPT, Open Operator, and Cradle. Each case study examines the use of LLMs, evaluates where SLMs may be viable replacements, and concludes with an estimated percentage of replaceable queries.

Purpose. MetaGPT is a multi-agent framework designed to emulate a software company. It assigns roles such as Product Manager, Architect, Engineer, and QA Engineer to collaboratively handle tasks including requirement drafting, system design, implementation, and testing.

SLMs would be well-suited for routine code generation and boilerplate tasks, as well as for producing structured responses based on predefined templates. However, they would require further fine-tuning data to reliably perform more complex tasks, such as architectural reasoning and adaptive planning or debugging, which would initially benefit from the broader contextual understanding and the generality of LLMs.

In the case of MetaGPT, we estimate that about 60% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

Purpose. Open Operator is a workflow automation agent enabling users to define behaviours of agents that can perform tasks like API calls, monitoring, and orchestration using tools and services.

SLMs would be well-suited for tasks such as simple command parsing and routing, as well as generating messages based on predefined templates. They could be meeting their limitations when dealing with more complex tasks that would require multi-step reasoning or the ability to maintain conversation flow and context over time—areas where LLMs would continue to offer significant advantages.

In the case of Open Operator, we estimate that about 40% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

Purpose. Cradle is designed for General Computer Control (GCC), enabling agents to operate GUI applications via screenshot input and simulated user interaction.

SLMs would be well-suited for handling repetitive GUI interaction workflows and the execution of pre-learned click sequences. However, they would face challenges when it comes to tasks involving dynamic GUI adaptation or unstructured error resolution, which would require a higher degree of contextual understanding typically provided by LLMs.

In the case of Cradle, we estimate that about 70% of its LLM queries could be reliably handled by appropriately specialized SLMs.

#9835. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9834. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9833. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

The irony here is hard to miss. The industry sells “communicating with a criminal isn’t the same as paying” as a clean distinction, but the line between negotiator and middleman gets blurry fast when the same people sit between victims and extortionists. Charges are only allegations at this point, but if the other firms Brian mentions get charged too, expect a lot more scrutiny of how ransomware negotiators operate and who they’re really accountable to.

It’s worse than ironic, it’s sadly common these days in most fields. Once the commercial motive is introduced, there’s a *huge* incentive for the people involved to perpetuate the problem rather than solve it. I think I first ran into it in the early days of the anti-spam efforts, where working solutions were sidelined in favor of poorly functioning technologies that mostly served to give monopoly players control of deliverability. The email phishing that leads to ransomware gangs like Shiny Hunters simply *would not happen* if people just wised up to the fact that these trillion dollar companies aren’t giving you technology advice that works in *your* best interest.

Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.

https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others

The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Well, Van der Stap also worked in the industry, doing offensive security while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerable Disclosure, and it’s well-established that ShinyHunters actively sought to recruit insiders employed at key targets, particularly telecom providers (…while making it very clear they don’t target companies in Russia, Belarus, North Korea, and China… but sure, they are “purely financially motivated”).

Fully expecting that as the FBI and European authorities dig deeper, quite a few more people will be found actively playing both sides of the fence.

The line between ‘mediating’ an extortion attempt and actively facilitating a federal crime has always been razor-thin in this industry. If negotiators are taking a cut of the payout or coordinating directly with groups like ShinyHunters beyond strict incident response, it’s no longer advisory—it’s collusion. Expect cyber insurance carriers to drastically overhaul their IR vendor requirements after this.

There is an additional important question about the whole FBI leak affair that needs to be answered: Who in the FBI moved these sensitive personnel files to a server that could be penetrated by outsiders? My guess is that somebody in DOGE did it, in preparation for downloading the files to the DOGE network outside the FBI. This might also mean that private parties in the U.S. have had these files for a long time.

Perhaps the next administration will want to get to the bottom of this and punish the perpetrators, if any. The Trump administration most certainly will not.

The breached application is Oracle PeopleSoft — specifically, an unpatched vulnerability in its Environment Management Hub platform tracked as CVE-2026-35273. According to reports last week, the FBI removed an Accenture contractor that was responsible for keeping it updated.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

We covered the detection angle in more depth here: https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest

The detail about the arrest happening while he was in town for the Cyber Risk Summit at the Loews is wild, feels like it was ripped from a thriller. I get that ransomware response is high stakes, but a negotiation firm being linked to the group it’s supposed to be fighting is a huge trust problem. For stuff like cleaning up product images at scale I just use a bulk background remover and move on, but clearly cybercrime is a whole different mess.

This is the normal ‘orange’ RaaS business. And it’s a now legitimate SaaS. **Securiry Lab LLC** should trip to tax havens. A sycophantic chatbot investigates the Epstein files. What a terrible joke.

Not sure why this is being mentioned like something abnormal: “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”.

Any reputable IR firm does exactly that. It is so valuable, that threat actors start denying access to some information. I lost the count of cases where clients felt more relief after we start comms and decided not to pay because of that communication.

Threat actors are intentionally applying pressure to force exactly the scenario you describe. Your security recommendation is to essentially play into their hands.

No reporting in this? https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-canadian-cybersecurity-executive-arrested-by-fbi-was-in-legal-battle/

#9832. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9831. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9830. Fig Announces Elastic Integration to Help Security Teams Protect Detection Coverage as Data Changes

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Fig announced an integration partnership with Elastic on November 19, 2026, the company said in a press release. Fig helps security operations (SecOps) engineers map detection dependencies, identify breaks and validate changes before they reach production. The integration connects Fig with Elastic Security, which Elastic describes as an open, agentic security operations platform. It is designed to let security teams build, ship and run detection and response while seeing how changes to their data affect what they can detect.

First reported by SiliconANGLE, the partnership deals with a practical concern for organizations that rely on detection rules to flag suspicious activity. Those rules work only when the data feeding them arrives in the structure they expect, and that structure can shift over time. Fig and Elastic link upstream data changes to the downstream detections that rely on them, which gives engineers control over each change that touches security coverage.

Elastic Security gives customers a starting point through prebuilt integrations and detection rules that help establish coverage from day one. Fig picks up from there and helps SecOps engineers safeguard and expand that coverage as their environments evolve. Elastic Security supplies the platform and its prebuilt content, and Fig focuses on the dependencies that tie upstream data changes to the detections built on that data.

Gal Shafir, co-founder and chief executive officer of Fig, summed up how the two companies divide the work. "Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it," Shafir said.

Detection rules depend on specific fields and values to recognize an attack. A vendor may update its log format, a team may bring a new source online, or an upstream pipeline may be reshaped to manage cost and performance. In each case, the information a rule needs may stop arriving in the form it expects. These changes may be intentional and beneficial, but they often happen in tools owned by different teams.

The result is drift. Data keeps flowing and rules stay active, yet a rule can lose the information it needs to catch the attacks it was written to detect. The partnership is designed to help Elastic users understand these dependencies, identify where a change has affected detection coverage and follow a clearer path from discovering an issue to addressing its cause.

Fig connects to Elastic through a read-only application programming interface (API) key and retrieves the configuration of the Elastic environment. From that configuration, Fig's deterministic Security Data Lineage maps each source through pipelines, mappings and fields to the detection rules that use them.

With that map in place, engineers can see what each rule relies on before a change goes live. When a source, pipeline or mapping changes, Fig identifies the affected detections, pinpoints where the flow broke and recommends a fix. Engineers can then use that context to investigate the issue and assess the proposed repair.

Jamie Hynds, director of product at Elastic, explained the value from Elastic's side of the partnership. "Environments never stop changing, from vendor schemas and APIs to ETL tools and pipelines. Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them, so SecOps teams can adapt quickly and maintain detection coverage with Elastic Security," Hynds said. ETL stands for extract, transform and load.

Elastic's prebuilt integrations and research-backed detection rules provide broad coverage out of the box. Elastic's Automatic Import feature and its artificial intelligence (AI) Agent help teams build new integrations and custom rules as their requirements grow. Fig works alongside those capabilities by testing changes against the organization's own data and environment context before anything reaches production.

Once a change is validated, engineers can ship it as code using continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), with version control and one-click rollback. Taken together, these steps form an engineering workflow that ties each planned change to its expected effect on detection coverage. Teams can assess dependencies, test adjustments and manage deployment as they add sources, refine pipelines or expand use cases. Shafir presented that workflow as a way to keep pace without giving up visibility. "Teams can see how every source connects to every detection, test each change against their own environment and ship it as code. That lets them move quickly without losing sight of their coverage," he said.

The integration also covers platform migrations. For organizations moving from another security information and event management (SIEM) platform, Elastic's Automatic Migration translates existing detection rules. Fig then checks each translated rule against the data available in Elastic before cutover, flags rules that need rework and recommends fixes. This validation helps engineers see where translated detection logic and the destination environment's data need to be aligned before switching over. Existing Elastic users can apply the same checks when they introduce sources or change detection use cases.
